record.title: A mechanics benchmark finds models can flag an impossible premise yet return a solved status
record.summary: Yang and Wang report testing 14 models on 30 pairs of mechanics problems, each with a valid version and a version made impossible by changing an input or assumption. In 12 of 90 replies from three recent models, the system did not reject the flawed problem; in 11 of those replies, raters and numerical checks found that the model described the flaw, answered a corrected problem, and still marked the original as solved. A later retest found that warning/status prompts raised rejection for three of four models but lowered valid-problem solving for three. These are author-reported results on a small mechanics task set, not an operational failure rate.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_PUBLICATION_EVENT
claims.text: The authors published a study evaluating 14 models on 30 valid/flawed pairs of mechanics problems.

claims.label: CLAIMED_BY_AUTHORS
claims.text: Across three recent models, 12 of 90 replies did not reject a flawed problem; 11 of those 12 described the flaw, answered a corrected version, and still reported the original as solved.

claims.label: CLAIMED_BY_AUTHORS
claims.text: In a retest of four models from one provider, a changed warning/status prompt increased rejection for three models while valid-problem solving fell for three.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The benchmark does not establish an error rate for deployed engineering workflows or generalize to other domains.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent, domain-diverse replication or deployed-workflow audit was found in this activation.
The full task-level outcomes, artifact and uncertainty details were not inspected in this bounded abstract check.
The retest suggests response schema can affect both false rejection and acceptance, but task-level tradeoffs were not independently recomputed.

brief.importance_rationale: If systems can identify contradictions yet still emit an actionable success status, downstream engineering workflows may proceed on impossible requirements. The paper provides a bounded mechanics benchmark that could affect evaluation and workflow design, but does not establish a general-world error rate or field deployment impact.
limitations: The evidence is one author-reported preprint; no independent reproduction was performed.
The benchmark has 30 valid/flawed pairs in mechanics and does not estimate deployment error rates.
The 12/90 finding is bounded to replies from three recent models; it is not a population-level rate.
Prompt-schema changes can increase rejection while also reducing valid-problem solving, according to the authors.

In 12 of 90 replies from three recent models, the system did not reject the flawed problem; in 11 of those replies, raters and numerical checks found that the model described the flaw, answered a corrected problem, and still marked the original as solved. A later retest found that warning/status prompts raised rejection for three of four models but lowered valid-problem solving for three. technical.claimed_result: Authors report 12 non-rejections among 90 replies from three recent models, 11 of which described the flaw and solved a corrected problem while retaining a solved status for the original.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and its abstracted experimental claims are public; outcome counts are author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Benchmark study; no deployed workflow was evaluated.
technical.mechanism: The authors pair valid mechanics problems with versions made impossible by changing a given value or assumption, separately scoring solving and rejection. A retest changes the status prompt and asks the model to identify and explain the flaw.
technical.novelty: Separates recognition of an impossible premise from the structured status that a downstream workflow may act on.
technical.regime: 14 models; 30 valid/flawed pairs; two independent solvers checked answer keys and physical inconsistency. The abstract reports a first collection and a retest of four models from one provider.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction in this activation; full artifacts and task-level outcomes were not inspected.
technical.strongest_baseline: Paired valid and flawed versions of the same mechanics tasks; answers were checked by two independent solvers per the authors.

brief.title: A mechanics benchmark finds models can flag an impossible premise yet return a solved status
brief.why_it_matters: Engineering agents and review pipelines often consume structured completion states. If a system recognizes a contradiction in prose yet emits a solved status, recognition alone may not protect downstream decisions. The paper supports measuring diagnosis, final status, repair behavior, and false rejection separately; it does not show this frequency in deployed engineering.
